title: Distance to the Nearest Marker
statement:
You get a string s and a marker letter c that appears in s at least once.

For every index i, find the distance |i − j| to the closest index j where s[j] === c. Return these distances as an array with one entry per character of s. Positions holding the marker get 0.

examples.why: Markers at 0 and 5. Index 3 is 3 away from the first and 2 from the second, so 2. The tail after the last marker only has one side to look at.
A single marker in the middle; the distance grows in both directions.

constraints: s and c are lowercase English letters
c occurs in s at least once
hints: For one index, the closest marker is either the nearest one on its left or the nearest one on its right.
Sweep left to right remembering the last marker seen. That gives the distance to the nearest marker on the left for every index.
Sweep right to left the same way and keep the smaller of the two distances.

explain.intuition:
The closest marker to index i is either the last one at or before i, or the first one at or after i. Searching outward from every index costs up to O(n) each, which is O(n²) for a long string with one marker.

Two sweeps fix that. Going left to right, remember the position of the most recent marker; that is the left distance for every index. Going right to left gives the right distance. The answer is the smaller one. It is the same trick as computing "nearest something" for every element in a row of DOM nodes without querying each one separately.
steps: Set last = −∞ (no marker yet). Sweep i from 0 up: if s[i] === c set last = i; store i − last.
Set last = +∞. Sweep i from the end down: if s[i] === c set last = i; replace the stored value with min(stored, last − i).
pitfalls: Using 0 or −1 as the "no marker yet" value. Positions before the first marker then get a small wrong distance instead of being left for the second sweep.
Only sweeping once. The prefix before the first marker (or the suffix after the last) has no marker on one side.
Searching outward from each index: correct but O(n²) when markers are rare.

solutions.title: Compare with every marker
solutions.idea: Collect marker positions, then for each index take the minimum distance to any of them.
solutions.time: O(n · m), m = number of markers

solutions.title: Two sweeps
solutions.idea: Left-to-right gives the distance to the nearest marker on the left; right-to-left gives the right side. Keep the minimum.

followups: The markers are now any of a set of letters. Does anything change?
Do the same on a 2D grid with several marker cells. Which technique replaces the two sweeps?
